aliases: Department of Defense research and development categories
entries.definition: Numbered United States Department of Defense research-and-development budget categories. They distinguish basic research, applied research, and advanced technology development before later prototype or operational stages.
A situation where available sources do not show something. It is not the same as proof that the thing did not happen or does not exist.
A short summary of a document, article, or report. It helps readers decide whether the full text is relevant before reading it closely.

Abstract coverage is the number or percentage of records in a dataset that actually have an abstract. Always show both parts, such as “742 of 1,000 records (74.2%),” because a percentage without its count can hide how much evidence is missing.
A checkpoint that decides whether a stage’s output is good enough to move forward. It should use stated criteria rather than a vague impression.
A practical check that a tool is installed and working from start to finish. Passing it means the setup is ready for the workshop task.
The share of all cases a model or coder got right. It can hide important failures when some categories are much easier or more common than others.
A relevance test asking whether the text represents the views, actions, calculations, or perspective of the actor the study is about.
A human decision process that resolves disagreements between coders, models, or reviewers. The adjudicator chooses the reference answer or label and should record why.

The Admiralty Scale is a way to rate both the reliability of a source and the credibility of a specific report. It is common in military intelligence, but the ratings still require judgment and should not be treated as proof.
A result calculated or summarized across many records, documents, or labels rather than judged one item at a time.

An artificial intelligence (AI) assistant is software that helps users write, search, summarize, code, or analyze information. It can speed up work, but a person remains responsible for checking important outputs.

Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH) is a structured method for comparing possible explanations against the available evidence. It emphasizes evidence that weakens a hypothesis, not just evidence that supports it.
A relevance test asking whether the text contains reasoning, interpretation, or intent, rather than only a bare factual mention.
The organized human and institutional capacity to interpret information. It includes trained experts, methods, seminars, libraries, and review habits that turn raw material into understanding.
A bias where an initial answer, label, or model output pulls later judgments toward it, even when reviewers believe they are being independent.

Annotation means adding labels or notes to pieces of text so they can be searched, compared, or counted later. Large language models can help annotate at scale, but people should check samples for accuracy.
A stored collection of labels created over time, often by humans. It can be reused for examples, training, or evaluation.
A workshop metaphor for how wide or narrow your search scope is. A broad aperture lets more possible material enter before you narrow it down.
A sign-in method where software uses a secret text key to prove it may access an online service. API means application programming interface.
A biological warning signal, often bright color, that advertises danger such as toxicity to predators. The workshop uses it as an analogy for signaling and deterrence.

An application programming interface (API) is a structured way for one software system to request data or actions from another. In a workshop, you may use an API to send text to a model or retrieve results.
The number of members involved in a relationship or event. A treaty with three parties has arity 3; a summit with four participants has arity 4.
A specific output being reviewed or used, such as a file, taxonomy, report, dataset, or interface state.
Applied to many items, usually with automated help, rather than tested on only a few examples by hand.
The process of deciding whether similar author names refer to the same person or different people. Poor disambiguation can merge separate authors or split one author into several identities.
How common a category is before considering any model or coder decision. High agreement can be misleading when most cases fall into one category.
Batch processing means running many items through a system together instead of one at a time. It is efficient for large workloads, but results usually come back later rather than instantly.

A Battalion Tactical Group (BTG) is a Russian military unit concept combining infantry, armor, artillery, air defense, and support at roughly battalion scale. In this workshop it is used only as a Russia-related military analysis term.
Benchmarking means testing multiple tools or models on the same task so their performance can be compared fairly. It works best when outputs are checked against a trusted human-reviewed reference.
Retrieval-augmented generation applied to scholarly literature. The system first retrieves real publications, then asks a model to summarize or answer using those sources.
A workshop tool that searches scholarly databases, gathers publication records, merges them, removes duplicates, and helps document the search process.
A searchable database of publications and citation information, such as titles, authors, abstracts, journals, and references. It usually describes papers rather than containing every full paper.
The quantitative study of publications using information such as titles, authors, dates, journals, references, and citations. It maps the shape of a literature rather than reading every full text.
A text format used to store bibliography entries, especially for LaTeX documents. It records fields such as author, title, journal, year, and publisher in a structured way.
The use of language-processing software to find and organize information in biomedical writing, such as research papers about genes, diseases, or drugs.

aliases: National Center for Biomedical Ontology BioPortal
entries.definition: An online repository of biomedical ontologies and controlled vocabularies. Researchers use it to find, compare, and map standard terms across biomedical fields.
A review setup where coders or models make judgments without seeing each other’s answers first. It helps measure independent agreement rather than copying or influence.
Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF) is a writing style that states the main point at the beginning. It is useful when readers need the answer quickly before reading supporting detail.
Boolean search uses words such as AND, OR, and NOT to combine search terms. It is precise, but it can miss relevant documents that use different wording.
In the Red Lines coding scheme, the passage in a statement that names the line, limit, or condition being set.
Checking difficult or borderline examples to see whether category definitions are clear enough to decide where each example belongs.
A chart that summarizes a distribution. The box usually shows the middle half of values, the center mark shows the middle, and the whiskers show the wider range.
Available to download in large quantities rather than one record at a time. This matters when you want to analyze a whole database at scale.
Burst detection finds sudden increases in how often a term or topic appears. These spikes can point to events, campaigns, or changes in attention, but they still need contextual interpretation.
The complete set of possible combinations made by taking one value from each dimension. For example, 3 × 3 × 3 produces 27 possible cells.
A category is a named group used to organize similar things. In analysis, categories help turn messy text into information that can be compared or counted.

A simplified biological rule describing information flow from deoxyribonucleic acid to ribonucleic acid to protein. The deck contrasts this known chain with social systems, where causal links must be estimated.

Chain-of-thought prompting asks a large language model to reason step by step before giving an answer. It can improve complex reasoning, but users should avoid assuming that every displayed step is correct.
A fixed identifier for a text chunk or passage. It lets an analyst trace a label, quote, or claim back to the exact part of the corpus it came from.
Chunking means breaking a long document into smaller pieces that a model or analyst can handle. Good chunking keeps meaningful text together instead of cutting through sentences or ideas.
A citation is a pointer to the source that supports a claim, quotation, or data point. It helps readers verify where information came from.
The surrounding text where one paper cites another. Reading citation context can show why a source was cited, not just that it was cited.

Claude Code is a command-line tool that lets participants ask Claude to help with coding tasks from a terminal. In the workshop, participants may use it to run or modify parts of an analysis pipeline.
A group of items that a method places together because they are more connected or similar to each other than to other items.
A method that groups similar records, terms, or passages together based on patterns in the data. It helps reveal themes that were not manually listed in advance.
A way to study collaboration by linking people who wrote publications together. It can show whether a field is solitary, team-based, fragmented, or internationally connected.
A method that links two works when later publications cite them together. It is used to map which authors or papers a field treats as related.
A codebook explains the labels, categories, definitions, and examples used in an annotation task. It helps different people apply the same rules consistently.
A person or model that assigns labels or categories to text according to a scheme.
An artificial intelligence tool that can work with files and folders, run commands, and help perform multi-step coding or analysis tasks from the terminal.
Cohen's kappa is a statistic that measures how much two annotators agree after accounting for agreement that could happen by chance. It is useful for checking whether a coding scheme is clear enough.
A command-line interface (CLI) lets you control software by typing commands instead of clicking buttons. It is often used for reproducible data processing and coding workflows.
An extra piece typed after a command, usually beginning with one or two dashes, that changes what the command does.

aliases: pipe a downloaded script into a shell
entries.definition: A command pattern where the output of one command is sent directly into another. Here, a downloaded install script is sent straight to a shell to run it.

Completeness means a set of categories covers what it needs to cover; mutual exclusivity means an item should not fit two categories at once. Mutually Exclusive, Comprehensively Exhaustive (MECE) is an ideal, but real data often creates difficult edge cases.
A confidence score is a number that expresses how certain a model says it is about an output. It helps prioritize review, but it is not a guarantee that the answer is correct.
A saved text value used by software to point to files, settings, or resources. If it points to something missing, the program may break even though the setting still exists.

aliases: Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project
Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone
entries.definition: Common datasets used in conflict and international-relations research. Each records events or cases using its own definitions and coding rules, which can make joining them difficult.
A confusion matrix is a table that compares model predictions with the correct answers. It shows correct hits, false alarms, missed cases, and correct rejections.

A context window is the maximum amount of text a large language model can consider at one time, including both the input and the output. Longer context helps, but important details can still be overlooked.
A fixed list of approved terms used by a database to describe records consistently. It can find relevant records even when authors used different words.
A shape is convex if it has no inward dents or holes. The workshop uses non-convex as a metaphor for a topic space with gaps or irregular regions.
A count of how often two terms appear together in the same documents or passages. Repeated co-occurrence can reveal themes in a field.
A map showing which words, terms, authors, or items appear together often. Connections are drawn when two items co-occur, helping reveal the structure of a literature or corpus.
A corpus is a structured collection of documents used for research or analysis. Its usefulness depends not only on size, but also on quality, metadata, and fit for the question.
A relationship in which two things tend to vary together. In a taxonomy, correlated dimensions mean some combinations are common while others are rare.
Corroboration means checking whether another independent source supports the same claim. It strengthens confidence, but repeated copies of the same original claim do not count as independent support.
A factor measured alongside the main thing being studied because it may help explain or compare outcomes.
Coverage describes how much of the relevant material, topic space, or target population is included. Low coverage can lead to blind spots even when the included data is accurate.
A bibliometric method that groups topics by counting which keywords or terms appear together across records. It is often used to build thematic maps of a research field.
A way to show how different taxonomy dimensions relate to each other, for example which combinations of categories often appear together.
Cross-tabulation is a table that compares two or more categories, such as source type by topic. It helps reveal patterns that are hard to see in a long list of records.

Comma-separated values (CSV) is a simple table file format where each row is a record and commas separate fields. It is widely used, but commas inside text can cause formatting problems if not handled correctly.
A dashboard is a screen that brings together charts, filters, and summary numbers for monitoring or exploring data. It helps users spot patterns without editing raw files directly.
A structured collection of evidence or observations that can be analyzed, shared, and reused.
A data type describes what kind of value a field can hold, such as text, number, date, or true/false. Correct data types make filtering, sorting, and calculation more reliable.
A data warehouse stores information from different sources in one consistent structure. This makes it easier to compare records that originally came from different systems or formats.
An open knowledge base extracted from Wikipedia’s structured infoboxes. It represents facts in a machine-readable form so they can be queried and linked.

A deductive taxonomy starts with categories defined before large-scale annotation begins. The categories can be tested and refined, but the main structure is set by design rather than discovered entirely from the data.
Deduplication is the process of finding and removing repeated content. It prevents reposts or copied items from being mistaken for many independent pieces of evidence.
A definition explains what a term means and how it should be used. Clear definitions reduce confusion when several people annotate or analyze the same material.
Pressure or threat behavior designed so the actor can deny making a direct threat. Because the threat is implied rather than stated, some coding schemes may miss it.
The total set a percentage or ratio is measured against. In recall, the denominator is all relevant material, including material you did not retrieve.
A version of data created from raw records plus rules or labels. Because it is derived, it can be rebuilt if the labels or rules change.
A family of formal languages for defining categories and relationships so computers can reason over them. They are often used beneath ontology languages.
A sign-in method where the terminal shows a short code and a web link. You open the link in a browser, sign in, and enter the code.
Devil's Advocacy is a structured technique where someone is assigned to challenge the prevailing view. The purpose is not to be contrary, but to expose weak assumptions and reduce groupthink.
A permanent identifier assigned to many scholarly articles, book chapters, datasets, and other digital works. It helps readers find the exact item even if the web address changes.
A dimension is a major axis for organizing information, such as time, geography, actor, or type of activity. A High-Level Taxonomic Principle (HLTP) is a top-level dimension in a taxonomy.
The requirement that one classification perspective should not automatically determine another. If two dimensions always change together, they may really be one dimension, not two.

These are frameworks for organizing national power and operating environments: diplomatic, informational, military, economic, and related dimensions. They are mainly used in military and security analysis contexts.
Disconfirmation means actively looking for evidence that would weaken or rule out a hypothesis. It counters the natural tendency to focus only on information that supports what we already think.
A document is a unit of source material, such as an article, post, report, transcript, or paper. It may later be split into smaller chunks for analysis.
Writing the boundaries, assumptions, and context of a topic before asking a model to help. It is meant to reduce the chance that hidden assumptions drive the output.
A molecular change that helps cause or sustain a cancer and can guide treatment choice. The deck uses it as an analogy for hidden mechanisms beneath surface labels.
DSPy is a Python framework for building and improving prompts and language-model workflows. Participants may use it to define a task, test outputs, and improve instructions systematically.
A scanning method that uses two X-ray energy levels to distinguish materials. The deck uses it to illustrate seeing the same object through different axes.
A connection between nodes in a graph. An edge can represent a relationship such as membership, borders, signed treaty, or any other defined link.
An edge case is an unusual or borderline example that does not fit the normal rules cleanly. Edge cases are useful because they reveal where definitions or categories need refinement.
Research material that exists but is not yet allowed to be shared, published, or uploaded under the rules governing the project or institution.

Embeddings are numerical representations of text that place similar meanings near each other in a mathematical space. They support semantic search, clustering, and other ways to compare meaning rather than exact wording.
Observed evidence from the real world, rather than argument, theory, or opinion alone. In the workshop, it means checking claims against collected material and measured results.
A category of thing that can be identified in text, such as a person, place, organization, disease, or chemical.
A workshop metaphor for using a taxonomy, publication data, or language models to scan a body of texts and reveal how knowledge, themes, or blind spots are distributed within it.
Text inside JavaScript Object Notation where quotation marks and special characters are written with backslashes so they can be stored safely. It can be decoded back into ordinary structured data.
The scientific study of animal behavior, especially in natural settings. The deck uses ethology to compare animal deterrence categories with strategic-studies categories.
Evaluation ex ante means deciding in advance what good performance will look like. It includes setting criteria, examples, and standards before relying on a model's output.
Evaluation ex interim means checking and adjusting an analysis process while it is running. It helps catch systematic problems before they affect the entire dataset.
Evaluation ex post means checking model outputs after they are produced, often against expert review or a known reference. It helps quantify reliability and identify recurring errors.
A final check that states what evidence was available, what was missing, and which claims most need human verification.
Evidence grounding means making sure an answer or claim is supported by the underlying source material. It is essential because fluent model output can still be wrong or unsupported.
An evidence span is the exact passage in a source that supports a label, claim, or decision. It makes annotation easier to audit because reviewers can see what the judgment was based on.
A workshop metaphor for the ordered chain of evidence-processing stages that supports the final reports.
A search method that puts words in quotation marks so the search engine looks for those words together in that exact order, rather than separately.

Exploratory analysis is the early stage of looking through data to find patterns, problems, or promising questions. It is useful for discovery, but findings should be tested before being treated as conclusions.
A maximum number of records a service lets you download or export at once or in total. It can prevent you from collecting a whole field in one step.
The F1 score combines precision and recall into one number. It is useful when you care about both false alarms and missed relevant items.
A publication failure where the peer-review process was faked or manipulated, for example through false reviewer identities or sham reviews. It undermines a journal’s quality-control process.
A clickable category, such as author, date, institution, or subject, used to slice a search result set. Facets let you summarize or filter records without starting a new search.
Falsifiability means a claim could, in principle, be shown wrong by some observation. It is a core idea in scientific reasoning because claims that cannot be tested are hard to evaluate.
A standard method for reconstructing three-dimensional images from computed tomography scan data. In the deck example, it produces noisier boundaries than the TV–TGV method.

Feature extraction means turning unstructured text into structured attributes, such as names, dates, topics, or sentiment. These features make it possible to compare and count information across many documents.

entries.term: Federally Funded Research and Development Center
entries.definition: A research organization sponsored by the United States government to provide long-term technical or analytic support, often outside normal commercial contracting.
sweep_terms: Federally Funded Research and Development Center

entries.definition: Zero-shot prompting asks a model to do a task without examples; few-shot prompting includes a few examples in the prompt. Examples often help the model match the desired format and judgment standard.
A field is one named piece of information in a record, such as date, source name, language, or label. In a table, fields often appear as columns.
A filter keeps only records that meet selected conditions, such as a date range, source type, or label. Filters help narrow a dataset to the part relevant to a question.
Fine-tuning means further training a pre-existing model on task-specific examples. It can improve performance on a narrow task, but it requires good training data and careful evaluation.
Low-level software built into a computer’s hardware that controls basic machine settings before the operating system starts.
A way of reasoning that starts from the basic features of a problem rather than copying existing categories, traditions, or source structures.
A 12-month accounting period used for budgets. It may not match the calendar year.
A skew in coverage or attention toward material related to the former Soviet Union, or away from other records. Here it marks uneven coverage in databases.
A language resource that organizes words by the situations or frames they evoke, such as buying, attacking, or negotiating. It supports structured analysis of meaning in text.
A large structured knowledge base of entities and facts that was later absorbed into Google’s knowledge graph. It is used in the deck as an example of industrial-scale knowledge representation.
The no-cost level of a service, usually with stricter limits or fewer features than paid plans.
A frontier model is a highly capable, general-purpose artificial intelligence model near the leading edge of current performance. The term is comparative and changes over time as technology improves.
A technical metaphor for locking the exact file contents before review, so later disagreement is not caused by people seeing different versions.
The complete contents of a document, not just its title, abstract, citation, or metadata.
A model output format where the model fills arguments for a named function instead of writing normal prose. Pipelines use it to get structured answers that software can read.
A widely used controlled vocabulary for describing gene functions consistently across species and studies. It helps biological findings from different labs add up.

Gerasimov, Chekinov, and Bogdanov are Russian military thinkers often discussed in studies of Russian strategy and operational art. In this workshop, they are used only as context for analyzing Russian military thought.
GitHub is a website for storing, sharing, and tracking changes to code and documentation. Participants may use it to download workshop materials or follow a shared workflow.
A decision label meaning approved to proceed or not approved to proceed. In this workshop, conditional approval is treated as not approved.
A browser-based Linux terminal provided by Google. It is used here as a fallback when participants cannot install the required tools on their own laptops.

A way of matching a smaller graph pattern into a larger graph while preserving the structure of connections. In practice, it asks whether the stored graph contains the relationship pattern you are looking for.
A way of using a computer through windows, menus, buttons, and icons rather than typed commands.
Research or analysis published outside standard academic journals and books, such as government reports, think-tank reports, working papers, or policy documents.

The grey zone is the space between routine competition and open war, where states use pressure, covert action, cyber activity, or information operations. In this workshop, it is mainly a Russia and security-policy context term.
Ground truth is a trusted reference set, usually checked by people, used to evaluate model outputs. If the reference is poor, the evaluation will also be unreliable.
Compressed using gzip, a common method for making data files smaller for download or storage. A gzipped file usually needs suitable software to open or decompress it.

A hallucination is when a language model produces information that sounds plausible but is false or unsupported. This is especially risky when the output includes invented sources, numbers, or causal links.
To collect records or documents from one or more sources into a working dataset. In this workshop it usually means gathering publication records for a corpus.
A short digital fingerprint calculated from a file or text. If the content changes, the hash changes, so it can prove reviewers are looking at the same version.
The body that assigns standardized names and symbols to human genes. Standard names let researchers know when different papers are referring to the same gene.
A hierarchy organizes items from broad to narrow levels. In a taxonomy, a broad category may contain more specific subcategories beneath it.
A metaphor for a complex topic that cannot be described well by one scale or category because many different factors matter at once.
A web page that displays data summaries, charts, or filters in a browser. Unlike a static image, an interactive dashboard lets the user click, filter, or explore views.
A web error meaning a requested page or file could not be found at that address. HTTP means HyperText Transfer Protocol.
Human-in-the-loop means people remain part of an artificial intelligence workflow by reviewing, correcting, and interpreting outputs. The goal is to combine machine speed with human judgment.

The Human Smell Test (HST) is an informal quality check where a person opens a small sample of model-classified items and asks whether the results look reasonable. It is fast, but it does not replace formal evaluation.
A hybrid taxonomy starts with a predefined structure but also records new categories that appear during analysis. This balances consistency with openness to unexpected findings.
A connection in a hypergraph that can include three or more members. It keeps a multi-party event as one object instead of breaking it into separate pairs.
A graph-like structure where one connection can link more than two things at once. It is useful for representing events such as treaties, summits, or supply chains involving several actors.
A broad word that covers several narrower terms. For example, “deterrence” can be a hypernym for more specific kinds such as deterrence by denial or by punishment.
An imaging method that records many wavelengths or energy bands instead of a simple color image. Different reconstruction methods can reveal or blur structures in the same underlying data.
A more specific word or category that sits under a broader one. For example, “deterrence by denial” is a hyponym of “deterrence.”

Hypothesis generation means developing testable explanations from patterns in data. Language models can suggest possibilities, but analysts must assess whether they are plausible, distinct, and supported.

aliases: International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision
entries.definition: The World Health Organization’s classification system for diseases and health conditions. It is used for reporting, statistics, billing, and comparing health data across countries.
Not meant to be changed after it is fixed. An immutable version lets reviewers know they are judging the same object over time.
A check of whether someone else can apply your category scheme without asking you what you meant. If they cannot, the scheme is probably unclear.
A journal included in a searchable database or index. Non-indexed journals may be harder to find and can be missed by database-only searches.
Indicators and Warning (I&W) is an intelligence approach that watches observable signs linked to a possible threat. It compares current activity with normal baselines and warning thresholds.
An inductive taxonomy lets categories emerge from the data during analysis. It is useful for discovery, but it can be harder to keep consistent across many annotators or batches.
Inference is the moment when a trained model applies what it has learned to new input and produces an output. For example, classifying a new text chunk is an inference task.
Ingestion is the process of bringing source data into a system in a usable format. It can include downloading, scraping, optical character recognition, cleaning, and standardizing files.
A written statement of what a stage expects as its input, such as required files, fields, format, or conditions before the stage can run.
Data that an employer, university, funder, or ethics rule limits you from sharing or sending to outside services.
A tool or procedure that determines what the study can detect and count. Here, a taxonomy is treated as an instrument because its categories shape what becomes visible.

The intelligence cycle is a model of intelligence work: defining needs, collecting information, processing it, analyzing it, and sharing results. Real work often loops back and forth rather than moving in a perfect circle.

entries.term: Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment
entries.definition: Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment (IPOE), also called Intelligence Preparation of the Battlespace (IPB), is a structured way to analyze terrain, actors, capabilities, and likely actions before planning. It is mainly a military planning term.

Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) refers to systems and activities that collect information, such as satellites, aircraft, sensors, and reconnaissance teams. The term is most common in military contexts.

A visualization turns data into charts, maps, or diagrams; an interactive visualization lets users click, filter, zoom, or explore. Interactivity helps investigation, but it can also make weak data look more persuasive than it is.
A join combines records from two tables using a shared field, such as a document identifier. Joins are powerful, but mismatched identifiers can create missing or duplicated results.
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a structured text format for storing objects, lists, numbers, and strings. It is common in application programming interfaces and model outputs.
JSON Lines (JSONL) stores one JavaScript Object Notation object per line. It is useful for large datasets because programs can read or write one record at a time.

Kent estimative language is a disciplined way to express likelihood in intelligence assessments using standardized probability words. It helps readers understand how confident an assessment is, but numbers and words still require explanation.

Keyword search looks for exact words; semantic search looks for similar meaning even when different words are used. The contrast matters when language, spelling, translation, or wording varies across sources.
A structured network of things and relationships, such as people, places, organizations, and events. It lets software answer questions by following connections rather than only matching words.
Ways of storing ideas so that categories, facts, and relationships can be compared or used by people and computers.
A label is a category name assigned to a text, record, or passage during annotation. Labels make qualitative material easier to sort, compare, and count.
A graph whose nodes and connections carry names or types. The labels explain what each thing is and what kind of relationship connects two things.
A large language model (LLM) is an artificial intelligence model trained to process and generate text. It can summarize, classify, draft, and answer questions, but its outputs need verification.
Level 2 (L2) and Level 3 (L3) are lower levels in a hierarchy beneath a broader top-level category. They usually represent increasingly specific subcategories.
A source that can only be used under a paid license, institutional agreement, or other access restriction.
A structured search and reading of existing publications on a topic to understand what has already been studied, argued, or classified.
LLM-as-a-judge uses a large language model to evaluate another model's output. It can reduce human workload, but it should be calibrated against human judgments.
LM Studio is a desktop application for running selected open-source language models on a local computer. Participants can use it to experiment without sending text to an external service.
A service that sends a request to one of several available computers or providers. If not recorded, the same model name may actually be answered by different hosts with different behavior.
Local execution means a tool runs on your computer. Local processing means the data stays on your computer and is not sent to an outside model provider.
A chart scale where each step represents multiplication, often by ten, rather than adding the same amount. It lets very small and very large counts appear on one chart.
A way of framing war as a tension among movement, holding positions, and wearing down the opponent. The case asks whether this pattern appears beyond the battlefield.
Markdown is a plain-text format for writing headings, lists, links, tables, and simple formatting. It is easy for both people and software to read.

Maskirovka is a Russian term for camouflage, concealment, and deception used in military and statecraft contexts. In this workshop it refers specifically to Russian doctrine and practice, not deception in general.
A workshop rule of thumb: start by looking at the whole problem before breaking it into parts. For literature work, it means first estimating the full body of relevant work.

aliases: Multi-Dimensional Taxonomy Development Framework independence test
entries.definition: A workshop-named test for deciding whether two ways of classifying material vary independently enough to be treated as separate dimensions or taxonomies.
The middle value when numbers are ordered from smallest to largest. It is often used instead of an average when very large or small values could distort the picture.
A controlled vocabulary used to index biomedical literature. It helps searches find papers about the same concept even when authors use different wording.
Metadata is information about a document or record, such as date, author, language, source, or location. Good metadata makes searching, filtering, and interpretation much easier.
A short, structured description of the research process: question, query, corpus, scheme, reliability, and blind spot. It helps readers inspect how the claim was produced.
The collection of bacteria, fungi, viruses, and other microorganisms living in or on an organism. It adds another biological layer beyond a person’s own deoxyribonucleic acid.
An intermediate product between raw evidence and final writing. In this case, it is a large evidence report that shorter arguments rest on.

Milbloggers are informal military commentators, often posting on social media about war or military operations. In this workshop the term mainly refers to Russia- and Ukraine-war-related Telegram commentators.
Missingness describes where expected data is absent, such as blank dates or unknown source types. Patterns of missingness can bias analysis if they are ignored.

Mixed methods combine quantitative approaches, such as counting and clustering, with qualitative approaches, such as close reading and expert interpretation. The combination helps balance scale with context.
A specific released version of an artificial intelligence model. Recording the build matters because a later model with the same general name may behave differently.
One request sent to an artificial intelligence model and its response. In this guide, batching documents changes how many texts are handled in each request.
The precise name or code a tool uses to select a specific artificial intelligence model. These names can change often, so recording the exact identifier supports reproducibility.
The company or service that runs the artificial intelligence model and receives the prompts and context sent by the tool.
Model selection is the process of choosing which artificial intelligence model best fits a task. The choice depends on quality, speed, cost, privacy, and how much review is required.
A detailed book-length study on a specific topic, usually written by one author or a small group of authors.

MTProto is the protocol used by Telegram clients to communicate with Telegram servers. It matters when collecting Telegram channel content through software rather than through the normal app interface.

Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) is a method for comparing options across several criteria, such as cost, quality, speed, and risk. It makes tradeoffs explicit rather than hiding them in an overall impression.
A classification scheme that describes the same item along several independent axes at once. Instead of one path down a tree, a case receives positions on multiple dimensions.
The workshop’s framework for generating, refining, testing, and validating taxonomies that classify the same thing from several independent analytical perspectives.

The Multiple Hypotheses Generator (MHG) is a structured method for producing many possible explanations by combining different answers to who, what, and why questions. It encourages breadth before narrowing to the most plausible options.
A deliberately tough review session where people or models try to find weaknesses, overlaps, missing cases, or bad assumptions in a draft taxonomy or argument.
The number of cases, records, people, or observations being counted or analyzed. A small N can make conclusions fragile because one missing or changed item may alter the result.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) automatically identifies names of people, places, organizations, and similar items in text. It can struggle with spelling variants, translation, ambiguity, and languages with complex grammar.

A near-duplicate is content that is almost the same as another item, with small changes such as a new headline, added sentence, or reposted excerpt. Near-duplicates can distort counts if treated as fully independent.
An example that should not receive a given label. Naming negative cases tests whether a category can actually exclude anything, rather than applying to everything.
A point in a graph representing a thing, such as a state, organization, person, document, or concept. Connections between nodes represent relationships or events.
Software that lets JavaScript programs run outside a web browser. The setup note says participants do not need it for this workshop path.
A filtering practice where records are kept and given labels instead of being removed. This lets you change decisions later and audit what happened.
Normalization means converting different forms of the same kind of information into a consistent format. Examples include standard date formats, consistent place names, or unified spelling variants.
A result showing that an expected relationship was not found. It is still a finding because it says the evidence did not support the proposed pattern.
The part of a total that is being counted in a ratio or percentage. It is the number being compared to the denominator.
A systematic distortion caused by what you are able or willing to observe. If your search only covers easy sources, your conclusions may reflect search limits rather than the real field.

A family of approaches that measure whole biological layers at once, such as genomes or proteomes, then study how the layers connect. The workshop uses this as an analogy for measuring layers of conflict.
A workshop metaphor for a taxonomy dimension that is trying to represent two overlapping ideas at once and should probably be merged or redesigned.
An ontology is a structured description of concepts and the relationships among them. Compared with a simple taxonomy, it usually says more about how categories connect.
The Observe, Orient, Decide, Act (OODA) loop is a model of how information turns into action. It is often used in military and competitive contexts to discuss decision speed and adaptation.
A publication status indicating that a work can be read online without a subscription or payment. Databases often let users filter by open-access status.
OpenAlex is an open catalog of scholarly works, authors, institutions, and related research metadata. Participants may use it to find or enrich information about academic publications.
A system for describing web pages and objects with structured properties so platforms can understand and display them consistently. The deck lists it as one corporate knowledge-graph effort.
A deliberately stated gap, limitation, or unfinished part of a pipeline, shown next to the result instead of hidden elsewhere.

Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) is intelligence drawn from publicly available information, such as news, social media, public records, and commercial imagery. Public availability does not remove the need for verification and ethics.
A category reserved for relevant cases that do not fit the current named categories. It prevents unexpected material from being silently dropped, but it must be monitored.

An artificial intelligence model whose internal learned numbers are made available for others to run or adapt. This differs from a closed service where users can send prompts but cannot host the model.
Dimensions that vary independently, so knowing a case’s position on one axis does not determine its position on another. In taxonomy work, they help avoid counting the same distinction twice.

Orthogonal plurality means using multiple perspectives that add different information rather than repeating the same distinction. It is useful when designing taxonomies, hypotheses, or prompts that should capture genuinely different angles.
An outlier is a record or value that differs sharply from the rest. Outliers can be errors, rare but important cases, or early signs of change.
A precise instruction for what a model or pipeline must return, such as columns, field names, or JavaScript Object Notation structure. It makes outputs easier to check, combine, and rerun.
Assigning too many labels to a text, including weak or indirect matches. This can make later analysis misleading.
A standard language for writing ontologies on the web. It lets people define classes, relationships, and rules in a machine-readable form.
The practice of splitting search results into pages. When collecting many records, you may need code to move through all pages and retrieve everything.
An organization or scheme that produces fraudulent or low-quality academic papers for publication. Paper mills can create fake data, fake authorship, or manipulated peer review.
Paragraph-based chunking splits text at natural paragraph breaks. It helps preserve meaning better than cutting at a fixed number of characters or tokens.
A paraphrase restates an idea in new words, while verbatim text repeats the original wording exactly. Use verbatim wording when exact language matters, and paraphrase when summarizing meaning.
Software that reads structured text and turns it into data fields a program can use. If the output format changes or breaks, a parser may fail or misread the result.

Paso Doble is a shorthand for an iterative workflow where a model proposes, a person critiques, the model revises, and the person validates. The value comes from repeated interaction, not one-shot automation.
A link between a patent and a scholarly work or another patent. Patent citations can show where research is connected to inventions, technology, or commercial applications.
Information about patents, such as inventions, applicants, dates, and classifications. It is a different body of evidence from scholarly publications.
The list of folders your terminal searches when you type a command. If a tool is installed but not on this list, the terminal may say “command not found.”
An academic journal where submitted articles are evaluated by other specialists before publication. Peer review is a quality filter, but it does not guarantee that a claim is correct.
Saved space where files remain available after you close and reopen the service, instead of disappearing at the end of a session.
The observable characteristics or behavior of an organism or system. In the workshop analogy, phenotype is the visible outcome produced by deeper layers.
A sequence of recorded steps that transforms inputs into outputs, such as collecting records, labeling them, splitting text, classifying it, and producing evidence.
A text format where values are separated by the vertical bar character, often used to show a path through categories.
A placeholder is temporary text or a temporary value used until the real content is available. It should be clearly marked so it is not mistaken for final information.
Playwright is a software library for automating web browsers. Participants or developers may use it to collect information from websites that require browser interaction.
A Windows command environment where users can type commands to manage the computer or install tools.
Precision is the share of items marked relevant by a model that truly are relevant. High precision means fewer false alarms and less irrelevant material for analysts to review.

Cancer treatment that uses molecular features of a tumor to choose therapy, rather than relying only on where the tumor is located. The workshop uses it as an analogy for classifying conflict by mechanism.
A formal way to write statements about objects and their properties or relationships. It underlies many knowledge-representation systems because it makes the meaning of statements explicit.
A Pre-Mortem asks a team to imagine that its analysis later proved wrong and then explain why. This helps identify hidden weaknesses before decisions are made.
Beliefs or expectations you bring before looking at the evidence. In the workshop, priors can shape the categories you build and therefore what you later notice.
Done by writing code rather than clicking manually in a website. Programmatic access lets you repeat searches or collect many records consistently.
A prompt is the instruction or question given to a language model. Prompt engineering means designing that instruction carefully, often with examples, rules, and output requirements.
A cost-saving method where repeated parts of a prompt are reused by the artificial intelligence service instead of fully processed again. It matters when the same long taxonomy is sent in many calls.
The full set of proteins present or produced in a cell, tissue, or organism. It shows what has actually been built from genetic instructions.

Provenance means tracking where a claim or item came from, including whether it is a primary source or a secondary source. Good attribution, citation, and traceability let readers verify the path from evidence to claim.
A search method that requires words to appear close to each other, not merely somewhere in the same document. It improves precision when simple AND would return loosely related results.

Prozrachnoye pole boya is Russian for “transparent battlefield,” the idea that sensors, drones, and digital traces make concealment much harder in modern war. In this workshop it is a Russia-related military analysis concept.

A biomedical text-mining system that identifies entities such as genes, diseases, and chemicals and links them to standard terminologies. The deck uses it as an example combining taxonomy and relations.
Pydantic is a Python library for checking whether data matches expected fields and data types. It helps catch malformed model outputs or files before they move through a pipeline.
A way to make an artificial intelligence model smaller or faster by storing its internal numbers with fewer bits. Low-precision formats can reduce cost but may change outputs.
A query is a request for information from a search system, database, or model. A good query states clearly what you want and may include filters or search logic.
A grouped part of a larger search strategy. The seed corpus uses bands so different parts of the search can be logged and sampled separately.
A tool mainly used to send questions to artificial intelligence models and compare their replies, rather than to act across files and folders like a coding assistant.
A query ledger records the searches, prompts, filters, dates, and decisions used during analysis. It supports transparency and makes it easier to repeat or audit the work.
A random sample selects items by chance; a stratified sample first divides data into groups and samples within each group. Stratified sampling helps ensure important groups are represented.
A rule that restricts how many requests you can make to a service in a given time. It can make large-scale downloading or model use slow or difficult.
The simple percentage of cases where two coders gave the same answer, before correcting for agreement that could happen by chance.
A three-part machine-readable statement: subject, predicate, object. For example, “Jaguar – type – Mammal” is a triple that software can query.
A displayed status showing how complete or ready a stage is. In the workshop, readiness is not the same as quality.
A file that explains what a dataset, code package, or project contains and how to use it.
Annotating the same material again, often by experts, to check or revise earlier labels.
Recall is the share of all truly relevant items that a model successfully finds. High recall means fewer important items are missed, though it may allow more irrelevant items through.
One of several broad, separate collection attempts designed to find as much relevant material as possible before narrowing it later.
A record is one complete entry in a dataset, such as one document, chunk, or annotation result. In a table, a record usually appears as a row.
A Red Team is a person or group assigned to challenge assumptions, plans, or analysis from an opposing perspective. The goal is better judgment, not winning an argument.
The step of removing or combining categories that capture the same idea, so the taxonomy does not count the same feature twice.

Reflexive control is a Russian strategic concept about shaping an opponent's perceptions so the opponent chooses the action you want. In this workshop it is used only in the context of Russian security thought.
A named kind of connection between two things, such as causes, prevents, treats, or interacts with. The label on the connection is part of the information.
Relevance screening is a first-pass decision about whether a text is worth deeper analysis. It acts as gatekeeping: it should avoid missing important material while reducing obvious noise.
Repeating a study’s test or analysis to see whether the original finding holds up. A finding that fails to replicate may have been wrong, fragile, or dependent on unreported conditions.
Reproducibility means another person can repeat the workflow and reach the same or comparable results. It depends on saved data, code, prompts, settings, and documentation.
A Request for Information (RFI) is a formal request for additional collection or reporting to answer a specific information need. It is mainly used in intelligence and military workflows.
The people, funding, institutions, tools, training, and routines that let a field keep producing knowledge over time, rather than a single short-term study or grant.
The formal withdrawal of a published scholarly work from the record because of serious error, misconduct, or unreliability. Retractions are counted in the deck as evidence of a trust problem.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a method where a language model first retrieves relevant source passages and then uses them to answer. It helps ground responses, but the retrieved passages and final answer still need checking.
A plain-text file format for moving citation records between databases and reference managers. Each reference is stored as tagged lines, such as title, author, year, and journal.
A usage limit measured over a moving time window, rather than resetting at the same clock time every day.
A workflow problem where an early decision about what text goes where controls all later results. If that first routing step is wrong, later analysis may never see the missing material.

RuBase is a research platform and document collection used in the workshop for studying Russian, Western, and Eurasian foreign and security policy discourse. Participants use it as a shared data source for exercises.

The Russia-Ukraine War Taxonomy is a structured category system for annotating material related to the war and its wider political and security context. It provides shared labels so results can be compared across documents.

Satisficing means accepting the first explanation or option that seems good enough instead of continuing to search. It is understandable under time pressure, but it can cause analysts to miss better explanations.
Microsoft’s knowledge graph project for representing entities and relationships used in search and question answering. It is listed as an industry example of knowledge representation.
A schema defines the expected structure of data, including fields, data types, and allowed values. Schemas help systems and people interpret records consistently.
Scope defines what is included and excluded in a project, dataset, question, or taxonomy. Clear scope prevents a task from expanding beyond what can be analyzed responsibly.
Automatically collecting information from websites, often by using software to copy pages or fields into a dataset.
A grouped set of related search terms, usually synonyms or closely related phrases, used together when building a search query.
A citation relationship one step removed from a direct citation, such as papers that cite papers that cited the original work. It is used to study broader influence through citation chains.
A seed corpus is the initial set of documents used to start an analysis, search expansion, or model-assisted workflow. Its selection can strongly shape what later analysis finds.
Semantic search finds material by meaning rather than exact words. It is useful when different languages, synonyms, or phrasing describe the same idea.
A vision and set of standards for making web data machine-readable and linked by meaning, not just displayed as pages. Ontologies and Resource Description Framework data are central parts of it.
Sentiment analysis estimates the emotional tone or attitude in text, such as positive, negative, neutral, or mixed. It can miss irony, propaganda style, and context-specific signals.
The command interpreter inside a terminal: it reads what you type and runs programs. Bash and zsh are common shells.
A separate file that stores added information about records, such as labels or scores, while leaving the original records unchanged.
A way to describe how much useful material appears compared with irrelevant material. In search, a high signal-to-noise ratio means many top results are relevant; a low one means noise dominates.
A data-processing failure where a record disappears from later results without an obvious error message, often because two labels or keys do not match exactly.
A search command that limits results to a particular web domain. For example, site:.edu asks a search engine to return pages from educational institutions.
A data-analysis metaphor for cutting the same collection into different views, such as by author, institution, country, or year.

aliases: Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms
entries.definition: A large clinical terminology used to record medical concepts consistently, such as diseases, findings, procedures, and body structures. It supports comparable medical records and research.
Influence achieved through attraction, persuasion, relationships, or legitimacy rather than force, threats, or payment.

A source is where information comes from; a source type is the kind of source, such as news, social media, official statement, academic article, or interview. Source type affects how evidence should be interpreted.
A very common word that a search engine may ignore, such as “and” or “the.” If an operator is typed in the wrong form, a database may treat it as a stop word.
A bias where people search where it is easiest to look, not where the answer is most likely to be. The workshop uses it as a metaphor for narrow literature searches.
Structured Analytic Techniques (SAT) are step-by-step methods designed to reduce common reasoning errors in analysis. They make assumptions, alternatives, and evidence handling more explicit.
SWOT is a simple framework for organizing strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. It is useful for quick strategic discussion, but it should not replace evidence-based analysis.
A review of publications that follows an explicit, repeatable method for finding, selecting, and analyzing sources, rather than relying on informal reading.
A system prompt is a high-priority instruction that sets a model's role, style, rules, or output format for a session. It differs from a normal user question because it guides the whole interaction.
Knowledge gained through experience that may be hard to write down as formal rules, such as practical judgment or know-how.
A taxon is one named unit inside a taxonomy, such as a category or subcategory. A taxonomy element is any defined part of that taxonomy, including dimensions, levels, or taxa.
Taxonomic annotation assigns detailed taxonomy labels to text that has passed relevance screening. It is a form of classification focused on placing evidence into a defined category system.
A taxonomy is a structured system of categories used to classify material. It reflects design choices, so what it can reveal depends on what categories it includes.
In this workshop, TE means taxonomy element: one named category or subcategory inside the taxonomy.
Team A / Team B is an adversarial method where two separate groups analyze the same question independently. Comparing their conclusions can reveal how assumptions shape judgments.
Telethon is a Python library for interacting with Telegram through MTProto. Developers may use it to collect or manage Telegram content in scripted workflows.
Temperature is a model setting that controls how varied or predictable generated text is. Lower values make output more consistent; higher values make it more varied but potentially less stable.
A structured table meant to show tensions, conflicts, or tradeoffs among findings or categories. In the case study, it is named as a product not yet built.
Using software to extract patterns, facts, or categories from large amounts of text that would be too much to read manually.
A chart that places topic clusters on two axes, usually how developed they are and how connected they are to the rest of the field. It helps identify central, niche, basic, or emerging themes.
A phrase for treating information as real-world objects and relationships, not just as words in text. For example, a person, event, or place is represented as a thing with properties.
In the Red Lines coding scheme, the passage that states what will happen if the boundary is crossed.
A chosen cutoff value used to decide whether a score counts as included or excluded. Re-thresholding means changing that cutoff later.
The ongoing work that happens between inputs and outputs: the activity or process itself, rather than what starts it or what it produces.
A set of measurements ordered by date or time, used to show how something changes across a period.
A token is a unit of text processed by a language model, often a word or part of a word. Token counts affect how much text can fit into a prompt and how processing is measured.
Awkward substitute phrases that can appear when text is automatically paraphrased to hide copying or machine generation. They are used as warning signs in some publication-integrity checks.
The Tradecraft Primer is a guide to structured analytic techniques used in intelligence analysis. In the workshop, it is useful as background for methods that make reasoning more explicit.
The full set of gene readouts active in a cell or organism at a given time. RNA means ribonucleic acid; this layer shows what parts of the genetic code are being used.
Transliteration converts text from one writing system into another, such as Cyrillic into Latin letters. Different transliterations of the same name can make search and entity recognition harder.
Treemaps and sunburst charts visualize hierarchical categories. A treemap uses nested rectangles, while a sunburst chart uses rings; both help show how parts fit into a larger structure.
Trend analysis tracks how topics, labels, or measurements change over time. It can reveal shifts in attention or behavior, but changes in data collection can also create false trends.
The quality of sounding or feeling true without enough evidence. The workshop uses it as a warning about persuasive outputs that still need checking.
Tab-separated values (TSV) is a table file format where tabs separate fields. It is similar to comma-separated values, but often handles comma-heavy text more cleanly.
A mathematical reconstruction method used to turn scan measurements into an image while preserving useful boundaries. In the slide, it is compared with a weaker reconstruction method.
A widely used version of Linux. In this guide, Windows users install Ubuntu through Windows Subsystem for Linux to get the kind of terminal the tools expect.
A system that links many biomedical vocabularies so concepts can be compared across databases. It helps connect different names and coding systems for similar medical ideas.
The unit of analysis is the thing being studied or counted, such as a document, paragraph, person, event, or organization. Choosing the wrong unit can distort results.
A cross-language system for labeling grammatical relationships in sentences. It helps language tools analyze syntax consistently across many languages.
A university-linked research center that works closely with the United States government on specialized long-term research and analysis.
An allowed output when none of the taxonomy labels fits a text. It prevents forcing every passage into a category that may not apply.
A vector database stores and searches embeddings efficiently. It is commonly used to find texts with similar meaning across large collections.
A computer feature that lets one operating system run another operating-system environment inside it, such as Linux running inside Windows through Windows Subsystem for Linux.

Voennaya Mysl, meaning “Military Thought,” is a Russian military-theoretical journal. In this workshop it is relevant as a source for studying official Russian military strategy and doctrine discussions.

aliases: Weltanschauung Analysis of Contemporary Kremlin Ontologies
entries.definition: WACKO is a project name used as a workshop case study for artificial-intelligence-assisted analysis of Russian strategic thinking. Participants can treat it as an example workflow rather than a general method name.

A Warning Problem is a documented intelligence question about a possible threat, including hypotheses, indicators, baselines, thresholds, and collection needs. It is mainly used in warning and watch-floor contexts.
A watch floor is a continuously staffed place where analysts monitor indicators and ongoing warning problems. It focuses on real-time awareness and escalation rather than deep long-form analysis.
A subscription database of scholarly publications and citations. Researchers use it to search literature, export records, and count publications or citations.
Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) lets users run a Linux command-line environment inside Windows. Participants may use it to run tools or scripts that expect a Linux-style setup.
A large lexical database that groups English words into meaning-based sets and records relationships among them. It is used in language technology and ontology examples.
A tool for saving, organizing, annotating, and exporting research references and portable document format files. It turns search results into a reusable personal or shared library.
